questions.question: Under Section 7 of IBC 2016, who can initiate CIRP against a corporate debtor?
questions.explanation: Section 7 of IBC allows a Financial Creditor (alone or jointly with other financial creditors) to file an application before NCLT to initiate CIRP when a default has occurred.

questions.question: What is the minimum default amount required to initiate CIRP under IBC 2016 as amended?
questions.explanation: The minimum threshold for default to initiate CIRP was raised to Rs. 1 Crore by notification dated 24 March 2020.

questions.question: Under Section 14 of IBC, moratorium is declared by:
questions.explanation: Section 14 of IBC provides that on admission of application under Section 7/9/10, NCLT shall declare a moratorium prohibiting institution of suits, enforcement of security interest, recovery of property etc.

questions.question: The voting threshold for approval of a Resolution Plan by the Committee of Creditors is:
questions.explanation: As per Section 30(4) of IBC, the CoC shall approve the resolution plan by a vote of not less than 66% of voting share of financial creditors.

questions.question: Under IBC, which creditor has the HIGHEST priority in liquidation waterfall?
questions.explanation: Section 53 of IBC prescribes the waterfall: (1) CIRP costs, (2) Secured creditors/workmen dues (24 months), (3) Other employee dues (12 months), (4) Unsecured financial creditors, (5) Government dues, (6) Remaining secured creditors, (7) Remaining operational/other creditors, (8) Equity shareholders.

questions.question: Under Section 8 of IBC, an operational creditor must send a demand notice to the corporate debtor and wait for how many days before filing an application?
questions.explanation: Section 8(1) of IBC requires an operational creditor to first deliver a demand notice of unpaid operational debt to the corporate debtor and wait for 30 days before filing an application under Section 9.

questions.question: The Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) must convene the first meeting of Committee of Creditors within how many days of his appointment?
questions.explanation: As per Regulation 25 of IBBI (CIRP) Regulations, the IRP must convene the first meeting of CoC within 14 days of his appointment.

questions.question: A resolution plan must provide for payment of at least what percentage of liquidation value to dissenting financial creditors?
questions.explanation: As per Section 30(2)(b) of IBC, a resolution plan must provide for payment of at least liquidation value to dissenting financial creditors, as per Supreme Court judgment in Essar Steel case.

questions.question: Which part of IBC deals with cross-border insolvency?
questions.explanation: Part II of IBC (Sections 234-245) deals with cross-border insolvency and is based on UNCITRAL Model Law on Cross-Border Insolvency.

questions.question: Under Section 59 of IBC, voluntary liquidation can be initiated by corporate debtor when:
questions.option_b: Company is unable to pay debts
questions.explanation: Section 59 of IBC provides that a corporate debtor may initiate voluntary liquidation when members pass a special resolution to that effect, subject to conditions.

questions.question: Fast Track Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (FTCIRP) has a timeline of:
questions.explanation: Section 55 of IBC provides for Fast Track CIRP with a timeline of 90 days from insolvency commencement date, which can be extended by 45 days (total 135 days).

questions.question: Which entity registers Insolvency Professionals under IBC?
questions.explanation: IBBI maintains the register of Insolvency Professionals. An IP must be enrolled with an Insolvency Professional Agency (IPA) and registered with IBBI.

questions.question: Operational creditors are members of Committee of Creditors:
questions.option_c: Only if there are no financial creditors
questions.explanation: Section 21(2) of IBC provides that operational creditors shall be members of CoC only if there are no financial creditors in the corporate debtor.

questions.question: Section 29A of IBC deals with:
questions.explanation: Section 29A of IBC specifies eligibility criteria for resolution applicants, including disqualifications related to NPA accounts, wilful defaulters, etc.

questions.question: Who appoints the Liquidator in case of liquidation under IBC?
questions.explanation: Section 34 of IBC provides that NCLT shall appoint a Liquidator for liquidation process of corporate debtor. The Liquidator must be registered with IBBI.

questions.question: Under IBBI (Insolvency Professionals) Regulations 2016, an IP must be a member of which entity?
questions.explanation: Under Regulation 3 of IBBI (IP) Regulations 2016, a person must be enrolled as a member of an IPA and registered with IBBI to act as an Insolvency Professional.

questions.question: The CIRP period under IBC is:
questions.option_c: 180 days extendable to 270 days, with 330 days as outer limit
questions.explanation: Section 12 of IBC: CIRP shall be completed in 180 days. NCLT may extend by 90 days (total 270 days). The overall outer limit including litigation is 330 days per Section 12(3).

questions.question: Under IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, a Public Announcement in liquidation must be made within how many days of appointment of Liquidator?
questions.explanation: Regulation 12 of IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations 2016 requires the liquidator to make a public announcement within 5 days of his appointment.

questions.question: An Insolvency Professional must register with IBBI within how many days of enrollment with IPA?
questions.explanation: Under Regulation 5 of IBBI (IP) Regulations, an enrolled member of IPA must apply for registration with IBBI within 30 days of enrollment.

questions.question: Under IBBI (CIRP) Regulations, the IRP must prepare Information Memorandum within how many days?
questions.explanation: Regulation 36 of IBBI (CIRP) Regulations requires the IRP to prepare Information Memorandum within 14 days of his appointment.

questions.question: The Liquidator must prepare the liquidation estate account within how many days of liquidation commencement?
questions.explanation: Regulation 32 of IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations requires the Liquidator to prepare liquidation estate account within 75 days of liquidation commencement date.

questions.question: Under IBBI (Voluntary Liquidation) Regulations, the Insolvency Professional must file the final report with NCLT within how many days of completion of voluntary liquidation?
questions.explanation: Regulation 13 of IBBI (Voluntary Liquidation) Regulations requires the IP to file final report with NCLT within 30 days of completion of voluntary liquidation process.

questions.question: Under IBBI (Grievance Redressal) Regulations, a grievance can be filed against:
questions.option_c: IBBI, IPs, IPAs and Registered Valuers
questions.explanation: IBBI (Grievance Redressal) Regulations provide for filing grievances against IBBI, Insolvency Professionals, Insolvency Professional Agencies and Registered Valuers.

questions.question: Under IBBI (Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process) Regulations, the base resolution plan must be submitted by the prospective resolution applicant:
questions.explanation: Pre-Pack Regulations require the prospective resolution applicant to submit base resolution plan along with the CIRP application under Section 7 for MSMEs.

questions.question: Under the Companies Act 2013, a "small company" means a company whose paid-up share capital does not exceed:
questions.explanation: As per Section 2(85) of Companies Act 2013 (amended), a small company has paid-up capital not exceeding Rs. 4 Crore and turnover not exceeding Rs. 40 Crore.

questions.question: An agreement without consideration is void EXCEPT when:
questions.option_c: It is made out of love and affection between near relatives and is in writing and registered
questions.explanation: Section 25 of the Indian Contract Act 1872 lists exceptions to the rule that agreements without consideration are void. One exception is: agreement expressed in writing and registered made on account of natural love and affection between parties standing in near relation to each other.

questions.question: Under Companies Act 2013, the maximum number of directors in a public company is:
questions.explanation: Section 149(1) of Companies Act 2013 provides that a public company must have at least 3 directors and maximum 15 directors. This can be increased by special resolution.

questions.question: A contract is voidable when:
questions.option_b: Consent is obtained through coercion, undue influence, fraud or misrepresentation
questions.explanation: Section 19 of Indian Contract Act 1872 provides that when consent to an agreement is obtained through coercion, undue influence, fraud or misrepresentation, the agreement is voidable at the option of the aggrieved party.

questions.question: Under Transfer of Property Act 1882, what is "mortgage"?
questions.option_b: Transfer of specific immovable property as security for loan
questions.explanation: Section 58 of Transfer of Property Act defines mortgage as transfer of an interest in specific immovable property as security for the payment of money.

questions.question: Under Sale of Goods Act 1930, a contract of sale is:
questions.explanation: Section 4 of Sale of Goods Act defines contract of sale as a contract whereby the seller transfers or agrees to transfer the property in goods to the buyer for a price.

questions.question: Under Partnership Act 1932, a partnership firm can be formed:
questions.explanation: Partnership Act 1932 does not prescribe maximum number of partners. However, Companies Act prescribes maximum 50 partners for a partnership firm (100 for banking business).

questions.question: Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) is governed by:
questions.explanation: Limited Liability Partnerships are governed by the Limited Liability Partnership Act 2008 and the rules made thereunder.

questions.question: Under SARFAESI Act 2002, a secured creditor can enforce security interest without court intervention if the account is classified as NPA and notice period of how many days has expired?
questions.explanation: Section 13(2) of SARFAESI Act requires the secured creditor to serve a demand notice giving 60 days time to the borrower before taking measures under Section 13(4).

questions.question: The Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act 1993 provides for establishment of:
questions.explanation: The Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act 1993 (now RDDBFI Act) provides for establishment of Debt Recovery Tribunals (DRT) and Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunals (DRAT) for expeditious recovery of debts.

questions.question: The Competition Commission of India (CCI) was established under which Act?
questions.explanation: The Competition Commission of India was established under the Competition Act 2002, which replaced the MRTP Act 1969.

questions.question: FEMA stands for:
questions.explanation: FEMA stands for Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 which replaced FERA (Foreign Exchange Regulation Act).

questions.question: In IBC context, when a corporate debtor goes into liquidation, the Liquidator must settle income tax dues within:
questions.explanation: The Liquidator must settle tax dues as per the applicable tax laws. Income tax claims rank as government dues in the Section 53 waterfall.

questions.question: Stamp duty is a tax on:
questions.explanation: Stamp duty is a tax levied on property transactions and legal documents. The Stamp Act varies by state in India.

questions.question: SFIO stands for:
questions.explanation: SFIO stands for Serious Fraud Investigation Office, which investigates serious corporate frauds under Companies Act.

questions.question: Which financial statement shows a company's financial position at a specific point in time?
questions.explanation: The Balance Sheet (Statement of Financial Position) shows assets, liabilities and equity of a company at a specific date, reflecting the financial position at that point in time.

questions.question: Under IBC, Fair Value of assets of a corporate debtor is estimated by:
questions.explanation: Regulation 27 of IBBI (CIRP) Regulations requires the RP to appoint two Registered Valuers to determine the fair value and liquidation value of the assets.

questions.question: Cash Flow Statement shows:
questions.option_b: Cash inflows and outflows over a period
questions.option_c: Financial position at a point in time
questions.explanation: Cash Flow Statement shows the cash inflows and outflows from operating, investing and financing activities over a period.

questions.question: In India, Accounting Standards are issued by:
questions.explanation: The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) issues Accounting Standards in India. These are now called Ind AS (Indian Accounting Standards).

questions.question: Current Ratio measures:
questions.explanation: Current Ratio is a liquidity ratio that measures a company's ability to pay short-term obligations using current assets.

questions.question: Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) is used in:
questions.explanation: WACC is used as a discount rate in capital budgeting decisions to evaluate investment projects.

questions.question: IBBI was established under which provision of IBC?
questions.explanation: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) was established under Section 188 of IBC 2016, and Section 195 provides for its powers and functions as a regulator.

questions.question: The chairperson of IBBI is appointed by:
questions.explanation: The Chairperson of IBBI is appointed by the Central Government. IBBI is a statutory body under the Ministry of Corporate Affairs.

questions.question: NCLT stands for:
questions.explanation: NCLT stands for National Company Law Tribunal, which is the adjudicating authority for IBC matters under Companies Act 2013.

questions.question: The IBC (Amendment) Act 2021 introduced which new process?
questions.explanation: IBC (Amendment) Act 2021 introduced Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PPIRP) for MSMEs through Chapter III-A (Sections 54A-54P).

questions.question: As per IBBI data, which sector has highest number of CIRP cases?
questions.explanation: As per IBBI periodic statistics, Real Estate and Construction sector typically has the highest number of CIRP cases due to capital-intensive nature and project financing.

questions.question: ABC Ltd. owes Rs. 5 Crore to XYZ Bank (financial creditor). ABC Ltd. defaults. XYZ Bank files under Section 7. NCLT admits the application. The Resolution Professional (RP) takes charge. ABC Ltd.'s promoter wants to continue managing the company. What happens?
questions.option_a: Promoter continues as management reports to RP
questions.option_b: Board of Directors is suspended and RP manages the company
questions.explanation: Section 17 of IBC: On the insolvency commencement date, the management of the affairs of the corporate debtor shall vest in the Interim Resolution Professional. The Board of Directors stands suspended and the powers vest in the IRP/RP.

questions.question: After CIRP fails, ABC Ltd. goes into liquidation. The liquidation estate has Rs. 50 Lakhs. CIRP costs are Rs. 8 Lakhs. Workmen's dues for 24 months are Rs. 5 Lakhs. Unsecured financial creditors have claims of Rs. 60 Lakhs. What do unsecured financial creditors receive?
questions.explanation: Section 53 waterfall: CIRP costs (Rs. 8L) paid first, leaving Rs. 42L. Workmen dues 24 months (Rs. 5L) paid next, leaving Rs. 37L. No secured creditors mentioned, so Rs. 37L goes to unsecured financial creditors on pro-rata against their Rs. 60L claim.

questions.question: XYZ Pvt Ltd (MSME) has defaulted on loan of Rs. 2 Crore. The promoter approaches a buyer who is willing to infuse funds. They want to use Pre-Pack process. What is the first step?
questions.option_a: File Section 7 application with base resolution plan
questions.option_b: IRP appointment and then CoC approval
questions.option_d: Wait for operational creditor to file
questions.explanation: For Pre-Pack PPIRP under Section 54A, the prospective resolution applicant must submit the base resolution plan along with the Section 7 application filed by the financial creditor before NCLT.

questions.question: Mr. Sharma (individual) has debts of Rs. 15 Lakh and assets worth Rs. 8 Lakh. He wants to file for insolvency. Under IBC Part III, which process is available?
questions.explanation: Part III of IBC provides two processes for individuals: Fresh Start Process for debts up to specified threshold and assets up to specified value, and Bankruptcy Process for higher thresholds.

questions.question: During CIRP of Tech Solutions Ltd, a contract is terminated solely because the company is in insolvency proceedings. The RP challenges this termination. Under which principle can this be challenged?
questions.option_c: Gujarat Urja principle on ipso facto clauses
questions.explanation: Under Gujarat Urja v. Amit Gupta (SC 2021), termination of contracts solely on grounds of insolvency (ipso facto clauses) violates moratorium under Section 14(1)(d) of IBC.

questions.question: IP Sharma is acting as RP in the CIRP of PQR Ltd. One of the resolution applicants is a company where IP Sharma's brother holds 30% equity. IP Sharma does not disclose this. Which Code provision is violated?
questions.option_a: Section 208 of IBC on professional conduct
questions.option_b: IBBI (IP) Regulations on conflict of interest and independence
questions.explanation: An IP must disclose all conflicts of interest. Regulation 7(2)(h) of IBBI (IP) Regulations requires IPs to comply with the Code of Conduct. The Code mandates disclosure of conflicts. Section 208 also sets professional standards. Non-disclosure violates both.

questions.question: During the look-back period before CIRP admission, ABC Ltd. transferred a property to its promoter's wife at 50% of market value. This transaction can be challenged as:
questions.explanation: Section 45 of IBC deals with undervalued transactions where assets are transferred for less than equivalent value. The look-back period is 2 years for related parties and 1 year for others.

questions.question: A power company in CIRP has a Power Purchase Agreement terminated by the state electricity board solely due to insolvency. The RP challenges this. The outcome depends on:
questions.option_a: Whether it is a financial contract under Section 14(2A)
questions.option_b: Whether the contract is ipso facto clause
questions.explanation: Under Gujarat Urja case and Section 14(2A), termination of contracts solely on insolvency grounds violates moratorium, unless it falls under the financial contract exception under Section 14(2A).

questions.question: Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PPIRP) under IBC is available for:
questions.explanation: Chapter III-A of IBC (Sections 54A-54P) introduced by IBC (Amendment) Act 2021 provides for PPIRP only for MSMEs (Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises).

questions.question: Part III of IBC deals with:
questions.option_c: Insolvency of individuals and partnership firms
questions.explanation: Part III of IBC (Sections 78-187) deals with insolvency resolution and bankruptcy for individuals and partnership firms.

questions.question: Section 43 of IBC deals with:
questions.explanation: Section 43 of IBC deals with preferential transactions — transactions where a corporate debtor gives preference to a creditor over others within the look-back period (2 years for related parties, 1 year for others).

questions.question: The outer limit for CIRP including extensions and litigation is:
questions.explanation: Section 12(3) of IBC provides that the overall period of CIRP including extension and litigation shall not exceed 330 days from insolvency commencement date.

questions.question: The Committee of Creditors must meet at least:
questions.explanation: Regulation 21 of IBBI (CIRP) Regulations requires the Committee of Creditors to meet at least once every 30 days during CIRP.

questions.question: A resolution plan under IBC must include:
questions.option_c: Both payment waterfall and management changes
questions.explanation: Section 30(4) of IBC provides that a resolution plan must include the payment waterfall, implementation schedule, and may include changes in management.

questions.question: Liquidation can be ordered by NCLT when:
questions.option_a: Resolution plan is not received within CIRP period
questions.explanation: Section 33 of IBC provides for ordering liquidation in multiple scenarios: no resolution plan received, CoC rejects plan twice, or applicant withdraws after second rejection.

questions.question: The primary duty of an Insolvency Professional under IBC is to:
questions.option_c: Both maximize value and act in fiduciary capacity
questions.explanation: Under Section 208 and IBBI (IP) Regulations, an IP has a fiduciary duty to act in the best interests of stakeholders and maximize value of assets while following the Code.

questions.question: Who is NOT considered an operational creditor under IBC?
questions.explanation: Operational creditors are those to whom operational debt is owed (goods/services, employees). Lenders of money are financial creditors under Section 5(8) of IBC.

questions.question: Financial debt under IBC includes:
questions.explanation: Section 5(8) of IBC defines financial debt to include a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against consideration for time value of money.

questions.question: In a CIRP with total admitted financial debt of Rs. 400 Crore, Bank A holds Rs. 260 Crore, Bank B holds Rs. 80 Crore, and Bank C holds Rs. 60 Crore. A resolution plan proposing a 40% recovery is voted on. Bank A and Bank C vote in favour, while Bank B dissents. Is the resolution plan approved by the CoC?
questions.option_a: No, unanimous approval of all secured financial creditors is mandatory under IBC
questions.option_b: Yes, because Bank A and Bank C together represent 80% of the voting share, which satisfies the 66% requirement under Section 30(4)
questions.option_c: No, because dissenting creditors hold more than 15% of the voting share
questions.option_d: Yes, provided the NCLT grants special dispensation for dissenting financial institutions
questions.explanation: Under Section 30(4) of IBC, approval of a resolution plan requires a minimum 66% voting share of the Committee of Creditors. Bank A (65%) + Bank C (15%) = 80%, which exceeds the 66% threshold.

questions.question: In the liquidation of Delta Steel Ltd., liquidation proceeds realize Rs. 100 Crore. CIRP and liquidation costs are Rs. 10 Crore. Workmen dues for the preceding 24 months are Rs. 20 Crore. A secured creditor with a relinquished security interest has an admitted claim of Rs. 60 Crore. How much will workmen and the secured creditor receive respectively under Section 53(1)(b)?
questions.option_a: Workmen receive Rs. 20 Crore in full; Secured Creditor receives Rs. 60 Crore in full
questions.option_b: Workmen receive Rs. 22.5 Crore; Secured Creditor receives Rs. 67.5 Crore
questions.option_c: Workmen receive Rs. 22.5 Crore; Secured Creditor receives Rs. 67.5 Crore proportionally out of remaining Rs. 90 Crore (1:3 ratio)
questions.option_d: Workmen receive Rs. 20 Crore; Secured Creditor receives Rs. 60 Crore out of the remaining Rs. 90 Crore without deduction
questions.explanation: After paying Rs. 10 Crore CIRP costs, Rs. 90 Crore remains. Under Section 53(1)(b), workmen dues (24 months) of Rs. 20 Crore and relinquished secured debts of Rs. 60 Crore rank pari passu (total Rs. 80 Crore). Since Rs. 90 Crore is available, both claims are satisfied in full.

questions.question: An MSME corporate debtor initiates a Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PPIRP) under Chapter III-A. The base resolution plan submitted by the promoters proposes a haircut of 35% on operational creditors and 20% on financial creditors. What action must the CoC take before approving this plan or opening competitive bidding?
questions.option_a: The CoC must approve it immediately since promoters of MSMEs have absolute exemption
questions.option_b: Under Section 54K, if the base resolution plan impairs operational creditor claims, CoC must require promoters to submit a revised plan or invite competing plans from third parties
questions.option_c: The base resolution plan is void ab initio and CIRP must immediately be ordered
questions.option_d: Operational creditors must vote with equal voting share alongside financial creditors
questions.explanation: Under Section 54K of IBC, if the base resolution plan impairs any operational creditor claims, the Committee of Creditors must require the promoters to improve the plan or invite Swiss-challenge competitive bids.

questions.question: During CIRP, the RP discovers that 8 months prior to the insolvency commencement date, the corporate debtor transferred commercial real estate worth Rs. 50 Crore to a director’s brother for Rs. 15 Crore. Under which section should the RP file an application before NCLT, and what is the relevant look-back period?
questions.option_b: Section 45 (Undervalued Transaction), look-back period 2 years for related parties
questions.option_d: Section 66 (Fraudulent Trading), look-back period strictly 6 months
questions.explanation: Section 45 read with Section 46 of IBC covers Undervalued Transactions. For transactions with related parties (e.g. director's brother), the statutory look-back period is 2 years preceding the insolvency commencement date.

questions.question: During CIRP, a resolution applicant submits a plan. The applicant is an entity where the promoter was convicted of an offence punishable with imprisonment for 3 years under the Companies Act 2013, and 5 years have not elapsed from the date of release. Is this resolution applicant eligible to submit a resolution plan?
questions.option_a: Yes, criminal convictions do not disqualify applicants under corporate restructuring
questions.option_b: No, under Section 29A(d), a person convicted for any offence punishable with imprisonment for 2 or more years is disqualified if 5 years have not elapsed from release
questions.option_c: Yes, provided a penalty fine of Rs. 1 Crore is deposited in the escrow account
questions.option_d: Only if the Committee of Creditors approves by an 80% supermajority
questions.explanation: Section 29A(d) of IBC specifically disqualifies any person who has been convicted for any offence punishable with imprisonment for two years or more, unless a period of five years has elapsed from the date of release.

questions.question: What is the maximum mandatory period within which Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) must be completed, including all extensions and litigation time?
questions.explanation: The second proviso to Section 12(3) of IBC mandates that the resolution process shall be completed within a period of 330 days from the insolvency commencement date, including any extension of the period of CIRP and time taken in legal proceedings.

questions.question: Under Section 12A of IBC, an application admitted under Section 7, 9, or 10 may be withdrawn with the approval of what voting threshold of the Committee of Creditors?
questions.explanation: Section 12A requires approval of ninety per cent (90%) voting share of the Committee of Creditors for withdrawal of an admitted CIRP application.

questions.question: Under Section 66 of IBC (Fraudulent Trading or Wrongful Trading), which authority has the power to direct that directors/partners shall be personally liable without limitation of liability?
questions.option_a: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI)
questions.option_b: National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT / Adjudicating Authority)
questions.explanation: Under Section 66(1) and (2) of IBC, on an application by the RP, the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) may order that any persons who were knowingly parties to carrying on business with intent to defraud creditors shall be personally liable.

questions.question: Does the moratorium declared under Section 14 of the IBC apply to a personal guarantor or corporate guarantor of the corporate debtor?
questions.option_a: Yes, moratorium halts all proceedings against both the principal debtor and guarantors
questions.option_b: No, Section 14(3)(b) explicitly states that the moratorium shall not apply to a surety in a contract of guarantee to a corporate debtor
questions.option_c: Yes, but only if the guarantor is an individual and not a corporate entity
questions.option_d: Moratorium applies to personal guarantors for a maximum period of 90 days only
questions.explanation: Under Section 14(3)(b) (inserted by 2018 amendment and confirmed by Supreme Court in State Bank of India v. V. Ramakrishnan), moratorium does not apply to a guarantor to a corporate debtor.

questions.question: If a corporate debtor has only operational creditors and no financial creditors, how is the Committee of Creditors constituted under Regulation 16 of CIRP Regulations?
questions.option_a: No CoC is formed; the IRP manages the process independently
questions.option_b: The CoC comprises the eighteen largest operational creditors by value, or all operational creditors if less than 18, plus one representative each of workmen and employees
questions.option_c: The NCLT appoints an official liquidator to represent creditors
questions.option_d: The CoC comprises only the top 5 operational creditors and shareholders
questions.explanation: Regulation 16 of the IBBI (CIRP) Regulations provides that where the corporate debtor has no financial debts, the CoC is constituted of 18 largest operational creditors by value, plus representatives of workmen and employees.

questions.question: Under Regulation 35 of the IBBI (CIRP) Regulations, 2016, how many registered valuers must the Resolution Professional appoint to determine the fair value and liquidation value of the corporate debtor?
questions.option_a: One registered valuer for each asset class
questions.option_b: Two registered valuers for each asset class
questions.option_d: One valuer appointed jointly by CoC and IRP
questions.explanation: Regulation 35(1) mandates that the Resolution Professional shall appoint two registered valuers to determine the fair value and liquidation value of the corporate debtor in accordance with internationally accepted valuation standards.

questions.question: Under Regulation 31A of IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, what is the timeline for the liquidator to constitute the Stakeholders’ Consultation Committee (SCC)?
questions.option_a: Within 15 days from the liquidation commencement date
questions.option_b: Within 30 days from the liquidation commencement date
questions.option_c: Within 60 days from the liquidation commencement date
questions.option_d: Within 90 days from the appointment of liquidator
questions.explanation: Regulation 31A(1) of IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 requires the liquidator to constitute the Stakeholders' Consultation Committee within sixty days from the liquidation commencement date.

questions.question: An Insolvency Professional must obtain an Authorisation for Assignment (AFA) from which entity before accepting any assignment as IRP, RP, Liquidator, or Bankruptcy Trustee?
questions.option_a: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI)
questions.option_c: Insolvency Professional Agency (IPA) where he is enrolled
questions.explanation: Under Regulation 7A of the IBBI (Insolvency Professionals) Regulations, 2016, an IP shall not accept any assignment unless he holds a valid Authorisation for Assignment issued by the Insolvency Professional Agency of which he is a professional member.

questions.question: Under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013, what percentage of the average net profits made by the company during the three immediately preceding financial years must be spent on Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR)?
questions.explanation: Section 135(5) of the Companies Act, 2013 requires eligible companies to spend at least 2% of the average net profits made during the three immediately preceding financial years in pursuance of its Corporate Social Responsibility Policy.

questions.question: Under Section 126 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, what is the contract of guarantee defined as?
questions.option_a: A contract to indemnify against loss caused by the promisor
questions.option_b: A contract to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person in case of his default
questions.option_c: An agreement enforceable by law between a creditor and debtor only
questions.option_d: A bailment of goods as security for payment of debt
questions.explanation: Section 126 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 defines a "contract of guarantee" as a contract to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person in case of his default.

questions.question: Under Section 58 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, in which type of mortgage does the mortgagor bind himself personally to pay the mortgage-money and agree that in default, the property may be sold?
questions.explanation: Under Section 58(b) of Transfer of Property Act 1882, in a Simple Mortgage, the mortgagor binds himself personally to pay and agrees that if he fails, the mortgagee shall have a right to cause the mortgaged property to be sold.

questions.question: Under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, how many days notice must a secured creditor give to the borrower requiring him to discharge in full his liabilities before taking enforcement action?
questions.explanation: Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act mandates a 60-day notice period in writing requiring the borrower to discharge in full his liabilities, failing which the secured creditor may exercise rights under Section 13(4).

questions.question: Under the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993 (formerly RDDBFI Act), what is the minimum debt threshold for a bank or financial institution to file an application before the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT)?
questions.explanation: By notification dated 6 September 2018, the Central Government raised the minimum pecuniary threshold for filing an application before the DRT under Section 1(4) of the Act from Rs. 10 Lakhs to Rs. 20 Lakhs.

questions.question: Under the IBBI valuation guidelines, what is "Liquidation Value" defined as in the context of CIRP?
questions.option_a: The value of assets as recorded in the audited financial statements of the company
questions.option_b: The estimated realizable value of the assets of the corporate debtor if the corporate debtor were to be liquidated on the insolvency commencement date
questions.option_c: The discounted cash flow value assuming business continuity for 10 years
questions.option_d: The enterprise valuation based on market capitalization of comparable listed peers
questions.explanation: Regulation 2(1)(k) of IBBI (CIRP) Regulations defines "liquidation value" as the estimated realizable value of the assets of the corporate debtor if the corporate debtor were to be liquidated on the insolvency commencement date.

questions.question: Which financial ratio measures the ability of a corporate debtor to service its total debt payments (both principal repayments and interest) from its operating profits?
questions.explanation: The Debt Service Coverage Ratio (DSCR) = (Net Operating Income) / (Total Debt Service [Principal + Interest]). It is the primary metric evaluated by CoC during resolution plan assessment.

questions.question: In the landmark Supreme Court ruling of Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank (2018), what principle did the Supreme Court lay down regarding Section 7 applications?
questions.option_a: The NCLT has broad discretion to reject applications if the corporate debtor promises future revival
questions.option_b: Once the adjudicating authority is satisfied that a default of the threshold amount has occurred, the application must be admitted; claims of set-off or counter-claims cannot be entertained
questions.option_c: Financial creditors must obtain prior approval from the Central Government before filing
questions.option_d: Section 7 applications cannot be admitted if an arbitration proceeding is pending
questions.explanation: In Innoventive Industries (2018), the Supreme Court ruled that once NCLT is satisfied that a financial debt exists and default has occurred, NCLT has no discretion and must admit the Section 7 application immediately.

questions.question: In Committee of Creditors of Essar Steel India Ltd. v. Satish Kumar Gupta (SC 2019), what did the Supreme Court hold regarding the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors?
questions.option_a: Commercial wisdom of the CoC is subject to merit review and revision by NCLT on grounds of fairness
questions.option_b: The commercial wisdom of the CoC is supreme and non-justiciable; NCLT cannot enter into the merits of business decisions regarding distribution of funds
questions.option_c: Operational creditors must receive equal percentage payments as secured financial creditors
questions.option_d: Resolution applicants must pay 100% of all dues to all creditors without exception
questions.explanation: In Essar Steel (SC 2019), the Supreme Court held that the commercial wisdom of the CoC is paramount and non-justiciable. Neither NCLT nor NCLAT has the jurisdiction to alter or overturn the business decisions of the CoC on fund distribution.

questions.question: In Mobilox Innovations Pvt. Ltd. v. Kirusa Software Pvt. Ltd. (SC 2018), what standard did the Supreme Court establish for "existence of a dispute" under Section 8 and 9 of IBC?
questions.option_a: The dispute must be proven beyond reasonable doubt before a civil court
questions.option_b: The dispute must be a genuine, bona fide dispute not a patently feeble or spurious legal defence, raised prior to receipt of demand notice
questions.option_c: A dispute is only valid if an arbitration award has already been passed
questions.option_d: Any oral protest made after receiving the demand notice qualifies as a pre-existing dispute
questions.explanation: In Mobilox Innovations (SC 2018), the Supreme Court ruled that under Section 9, NCLT only needs to see whether there exists a plausible contention requiring investigation (pre-existing dispute) raised before receipt of the Section 8 demand notice.

questions.question: Under Section 9(3)(b) of the IBC, which of the following documents is an Operational Creditor mandatory required to furnish along with the application?
questions.option_a: A copy of the certificate from financial institutions maintaining accounts of the corporate debtor
questions.option_b: An affidavit to the effect that there is no notice given by the corporate debtor relating to a dispute of the unpaid operational debt
questions.option_c: A written approval from 66% of all operational creditors
questions.option_d: A bank guarantee equivalent to 10% of the operational debt claimed
questions.explanation: Section 9(3)(b) of IBC mandates that the operational creditor must file an affidavit stating that there is no notice of an existing dispute given by the corporate debtor regarding the unpaid operational debt.

questions.question: Under Section 30(2)(b) of IBC, as amended, the payment of debts of operational creditors under a resolution plan shall not be less than:
questions.option_a: 100% of their verified operational claims within 30 days
questions.option_b: The amount that would have been paid to them in the event of a liquidation under Section 53, or the amount payable if resolution proceeds were distributed under Section 53 order of priority, whichever is higher
questions.option_c: The amount determined by the Resolution Professional in his sole administrative discretion
questions.option_d: Equal percentage share as secured financial creditors
questions.explanation: Section 30(2)(b) stipulates that operational creditors must receive at least the liquidation value under Section 53 or the amount payable if proceeds were distributed in accordance with Section 53(1) priority, whichever is higher.

questions.question: Under Section 43 of the IBC, what is the relevant "look-back" period for preferential transactions entered into with related parties?
questions.option_a: One year preceding the insolvency commencement date
questions.option_b: Two years preceding the insolvency commencement date
questions.option_c: Three years preceding the insolvency commencement date
questions.option_d: Five years preceding the insolvency commencement date
questions.explanation: Under Section 43(4) of IBC, the look-back period for preferential transactions is 2 years preceding the insolvency commencement date for related parties, and 1 year for non-related parties.

questions.question: Under Section 45 of IBC, an undervalued transaction can be challenged if the corporate debtor transferred assets for a consideration significantly less than the value provided by the debtor within:
questions.option_a: 6 months for non-related parties and 1 year for related parties
questions.option_b: 1 year for non-related parties and 2 years for related parties preceding the insolvency commencement date
questions.option_c: 3 years for all parties without exception
questions.explanation: Section 46(1) of IBC prescribes the look-back period for undervalued transactions as 1 year for unrelated parties and 2 years for related parties prior to the insolvency commencement date.

questions.question: What is the maximum timeline prescribed under Section 54L of IBC for the completion of the Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PPIRP)?
questions.option_b: 120 days from commencement (90 days for RP submission + 30 days for NCLT approval)
questions.explanation: Under Section 54D and 54L, the PPIRP must be completed within 120 days from pre-packaged insolvency commencement date, with 90 days allowed for RP to submit the plan to Adjudicating Authority and 30 days for AA to approve/reject.

questions.question: Under Section 21(2) proviso of IBC, a financial creditor who is a "related party" of the corporate debtor:
questions.option_a: Cannot submit any claim in CIRP
questions.option_b: Shall not have any right of representation, participation or voting in a meeting of the Committee of Creditors
questions.option_c: Has voting rights limited to a maximum of 10%
questions.option_d: May vote provided NCLT grants prior leave
questions.explanation: Section 21(2) first proviso clearly mandates that a financial creditor who is a related party of the corporate debtor shall not have any right of representation, participation or voting in a meeting of the CoC.

questions.question: Which of the following transactions is explicitly EXEMPT from the moratorium provisions of Section 14(1) as per Section 14(3)?
questions.option_a: Execution of a decree by a money lender against corporate debtor assets
questions.option_b: A surety in a contract of guarantee to a corporate debtor
questions.option_c: Filing of a new civil suit for breach of contract against the debtor
questions.option_d: Foreclosure of mortgage on the registered corporate office
questions.explanation: Section 14(3)(b) provides that the moratorium under Section 14(1) does not apply to a surety in a contract of guarantee to a corporate debtor (reaffirmed by the Supreme Court in SBI v. V. Ramakrishnan).

questions.question: Under Section 33(5) of IBC, subject to Section 52, when a liquidation order has been passed, what is the consequence regarding legal suits?
questions.option_a: All existing suits automatically continue before the civil court
questions.option_b: No suit or other legal proceeding shall be instituted by or against the corporate debtor, except with prior approval of the Adjudicating Authority
questions.option_c: The liquidator cannot file any suits even for recovery of debts
questions.option_d: The liquidator must obtain approval from 75% of creditors before defending suits
questions.explanation: Section 33(5) provides that on passing of a liquidation order, no suit or other legal proceeding shall be instituted by or against the corporate debtor, provided that a suit may be instituted by the liquidator on behalf of the debtor with prior approval of NCLT.

questions.question: Under Part III Chapter II (Fresh Start Process) of IBC, what is the maximum qualifying debt threshold for an individual to apply for Fresh Start under Section 80?
questions.explanation: Under Section 80(2)(c) of IBC, the qualifying debt of an individual applying for Fresh Start Process shall not exceed Rs. 35,000 (with gross annual income not exceeding Rs. 60,000 and assets not exceeding Rs. 20,000).

questions.question: Who is eligible to initiate Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PPIRP) under Section 54A of the IBC?
questions.option_a: Any corporate debtor with debt over Rs. 100 Crore
questions.option_b: Corporate debtors classified as Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) under MSMED Act 2006
questions.option_c: Only listed public companies undergoing financial distress
questions.option_d: Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) with assets over Rs. 500 Crore
questions.explanation: Section 54A(1) limits PPIRP eligibility exclusively to corporate debtors that are micro, small or medium enterprises under sub-section (1) of section 7 of the MSMED Act, 2006.

questions.question: What is the minimum voting share of financial creditors required to replace an Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) with a Resolution Professional under Section 22(2)?
questions.explanation: Section 22(2) specifies that the Committee of Creditors may, in its first meeting, by a majority vote of not less than 66% of voting share, resolve to appoint the IRP as RP or replace the IRP.

questions.question: In Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Ltd. v. Amit Gupta (2021), what did the Supreme Court hold regarding NCLT’s jurisdiction under Section 60(5) and termination of contracts during CIRP?
questions.option_a: NCLT has no jurisdiction over contractual disputes between private parties
questions.option_b: NCLT can restrain termination of a contract if the termination is solely grounded on insolvency (ipso facto clause) and central to corporate debtor’s survival as a going concern
questions.option_c: Contract termination is an absolute right of non-debtor counterparties
questions.option_d: Only High Courts under Article 226 can intervene in statutory contracts during CIRP
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court ruled that NCLT under Section 60(5)(c) has jurisdiction to restrain termination of a Power Purchase Agreement where termination is solely grounded on the CIRP initiation and is crucial to keeping the CD as a going concern.

questions.question: Under Regulation 35A of the IBBI (CIRP) Regulations, by which day from insolvency commencement date must the Resolution Professional form an opinion on avoidance transactions (preferential, undervalued, fraudulent)?
questions.explanation: Regulation 35A(1) mandates the RP to form an opinion on avoidance transactions on or before the 75th day of the insolvency commencement date, make a determination by the 115th day, and file an application before NCLT by the 135th day.

questions.question: Under Regulation 36A of IBBI (CIRP) Regulations, within how many days from insolvency commencement must the RP publish Form G inviting Expression of Interest (EOI)?
questions.explanation: Regulation 36A(1) requires the Resolution Professional to publish brief particulars of the invitation for expression of interest in Form G not later than the 60th day from the insolvency commencement date.

questions.question: Under Regulation 44 of IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016, what is the standard time period within which the liquidator shall liquidate the corporate debtor?
questions.explanation: Regulation 44(1) provides that the liquidator shall liquidate the corporate debtor within a period of one year from the liquidation commencement date (amended from earlier two years).

questions.question: Under the Code of Conduct in First Schedule to IBBI (Insolvency Professionals) Regulations, 2016, an Insolvency Professional must NOT:
questions.option_b: Accept any gifts, hospitality or advantages from corporate debtor or related parties that could influence professional judgment
questions.option_c: Appoint registered valuers to value assets
questions.option_d: Engage legal counsel to represent CIRP proceedings before NCLT
questions.explanation: Clause 9 and 10 of the IP Code of Conduct strictly prohibit accepting gifts, hospitality, or any financial advantage that may compromise independence, impartiality, or objectivity.

questions.question: Under Regulation 27 of IBBI (CIRP) Regulations, how many registered valuers must the Resolution Professional appoint within 47 days of insolvency commencement?
questions.option_a: One registered valuer for all asset classes
questions.option_b: Two registered valuers to determine the fair value and liquidation value of the corporate debtor
questions.option_c: Three registered valuers (one nominated by debtor, two by CoC)
questions.option_d: No valuers unless requested by 51% of CoC
questions.explanation: Regulation 27 mandates the RP to appoint two registered valuers within 47 days of the insolvency commencement date to determine the fair value and the liquidation value of the corporate debtor.

questions.question: Under Regulation 31A of IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, what is the Stakeholders’ Consultation Committee (SCC) role during liquidation?
questions.option_a: It has veto power over all liquidator decisions including sales
questions.option_b: It advises the liquidator on matters relating to sale of assets, appointment of professionals, and fee structures, though its advice is non-binding
questions.option_c: It replaces the liquidator automatically if liquidation exceeds 180 days
questions.option_d: It consists only of operational creditors and employees
questions.explanation: Regulation 31A requires constitution of the Stakeholders’ Consultation Committee (SCC) to advise the liquidator. While liquidator must record reasons if rejecting SCC advice, SCC is primarily advisory.

questions.question: Under Section 59 of IBC read with IBBI (Voluntary Liquidation) Regulations, which of the following is a mandatory condition for initiating voluntary liquidation?
questions.option_a: The corporate debtor must have defaulted on financial debts
questions.option_b: A declaration from majority of directors verified by affidavit that the company has no debt or can pay debts in full, and is not being liquidated to defraud anyone
questions.option_c: Prior approval of 75% of operational creditors in value
questions.option_d: Permission from the Reserve Bank of India
questions.explanation: Section 59(3)(a) requires a declaration by a majority of directors verified by affidavit confirming that company has no debt or will be able to pay debts in full, and liquidation is not to defraud any person.

questions.question: Under Section 54C of IBC, who prepares and presents the "Base Resolution Plan" in a Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process?
questions.explanation: In PPIRP under Section 54K, the corporate debtor submits the base resolution plan to the resolution professional, who presents it to the Committee of Creditors for consideration.

questions.question: An Insolvency Professional Agency (IPA) is regulated by IBBI under:
questions.option_a: Section 196 and Part IV of the IBC 2016
questions.explanation: Insolvency Professional Agencies (IPAs) are statutory regulatory bodies registered under Section 201 and regulated under Part IV of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016.

questions.question: Under Regulation 38(1) of IBBI (CIRP) Regulations, what priority must a resolution plan ensure for payment of insolvency resolution process costs?
questions.option_a: Payment equal to unsecured financial creditors within 1 year
questions.option_b: Payment in priority to the payment of other debts of the corporate debtor
questions.option_c: Payment within 5 years in quarterly instalments
questions.option_d: Payment only after full settlement of secured lenders
questions.explanation: Regulation 38(1) mandates that the amount payable under a resolution plan to the insolvency resolution process costs shall be paid in priority to the payment of other debts of the corporate debtor.

questions.question: Under Section 186 of Companies Act 2013, a company cannot give loans or guarantees exceeding 60% of paid-up share capital, free reserves and securities premium or 100% of free reserves and securities premium without:
questions.option_a: Prior approval of the Board of Directors only
questions.option_b: Prior approval by special resolution passed in general meeting
questions.option_c: Permission from National Company Law Tribunal
questions.explanation: Under Section 186(3) of Companies Act 2013, where the aggregate of loans, guarantees or investments exceeds the prescribed limits (60%/100%), prior authorization by a special resolution passed in a general meeting is mandatory.

questions.question: Under Section 134(5) of Companies Act 2013, what is included in the Directors’ Responsibility Statement?
questions.option_a: Guarantee of 15% dividend to equity shareholders
questions.option_b: Statement that applicable accounting standards have been followed, accounting policies applied consistently, and adequate internal financial controls were operating effectively
questions.option_c: Undertaking that no director has taken loans from any commercial bank
questions.option_d: Declaration that the company has no operational creditors
questions.explanation: Section 134(5) specifies that the Directors’ Responsibility Statement must state that applicable accounting standards were followed, proper accounting policies selected and applied, and adequate internal financial controls were in place.

questions.question: Under Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act 1872, the liability of the surety is:
questions.option_a: Secondary and contingent upon court decree against principal debtor
questions.option_b: Co-extensive with that of the principal debtor, unless otherwise provided by the contract
questions.option_c: Limited strictly to 50% of the principal debt
questions.option_d: Extinguished as soon as moratorium begins under IBC
questions.explanation: Section 128 of Indian Contract Act 1872 states: "The liability of the surety is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor, unless it is otherwise provided by the contract." Creditor can sue surety directly without exhausting remedies against debtor.

questions.question: Under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act 1872, an agreement to do an act impossible in itself is:
questions.explanation: Section 56 (first paragraph) of Contract Act 1872 states: "An agreement to do an act impossible in itself is void." This is the foundation of doctrine of frustration.

questions.question: Under Section 58(f) of Transfer of Property Act 1882, a "Mortgage by deposit of title deeds" (Equitable Mortgage) is created by:
questions.option_a: A registered mortgage deed with two attesting witnesses
questions.option_b: Delivering to a creditor or his agent documents of title to immovable property with intent to create a security thereon
questions.option_c: Transferring physical possession of the mortgaged property to the lender
questions.option_d: Registering a hypothecation deed with ROC within 30 days
questions.explanation: Section 58(f) provides that where a person delivers to a creditor documents of title to immovable property, with intent to create a security thereon, the transaction is called a mortgage by deposit of title deeds.

questions.question: Under Section 47 of the Sale of Goods Act 1930, an unpaid seller who is in possession of goods is entitled to retain possession (Seller’s Lien) until payment when:
questions.option_a: Goods have been sold without any stipulation as to credit
questions.option_b: Goods have been sold on credit, but the credit term has expired
questions.explanation: Section 47(1) of Sale of Goods Act allows an unpaid seller to exercise right of lien in all three circumstances: sold without stipulation as to credit, sold on credit where term expired, or where buyer becomes insolvent.

questions.question: Under Section 7 of Limited Liability Partnership Act 2008, every LLP shall have at least:
questions.option_a: One designated partner who must be a Chartered Accountant
questions.option_b: Two designated partners who are individuals, at least one of whom is resident in India
questions.option_c: Three designated partners including one nominee of financial creditors
questions.option_d: Five partners with minimum capital of Rs. 10 Lakhs
questions.explanation: Section 7(1) of LLP Act 2008 specifies that every LLP shall have at least two designated partners who are individuals, and at least one of them shall be a resident in India.

questions.question: Under Section 69 of the Indian Partnership Act 1932, what is the effect of non-registration of a partnership firm?
questions.option_a: The partnership firm is declared illegal and void
questions.option_b: No suit to enforce a right arising from a contract can be instituted in any court by or on behalf of the firm against any third party unless the firm is registered
questions.option_c: Partners cannot share profits and losses
questions.option_d: The firm cannot borrow loans from commercial banks
questions.explanation: Section 69 of Partnership Act bars an unregistered firm or its partners from filing a civil suit to enforce contractual rights against third parties, although third parties can still sue the unregistered firm.

questions.question: Under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act 2002, how much notice period must a secured creditor give to the defaulting borrower before taking measures under Section 13(4)?
questions.explanation: Section 13(2) of SARFAESI Act 2002 mandates that the secured creditor must give 60 days’ notice in writing requiring the borrower to discharge in full his liabilities before taking enforcement action under Section 13(4).

questions.question: What is the relationship between SARFAESI Act 2002 and IBC 2016 in terms of override / supremacy?
questions.option_a: SARFAESI Act overrides IBC 2016 as it deals with secured creditors
questions.option_b: IBC Section 238 has an overriding effect over inconsistent provisions in all other laws including SARFAESI Act
questions.option_c: Both laws have equal concurrent jurisdiction
questions.option_d: Secured creditors can enforce SARFAESI even during Section 14 moratorium
questions.explanation: Section 238 of IBC contains a non-obstante clause that gives the IBC overriding effect over anything inconsistent contained in any other law for the time being in force, including SARFAESI Act (confirmed in Pegasus Assets v. Haryana Concast).

questions.question: Under the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act 1993 (RDB Act / RDDBFI), what is the minimum pecuniary threshold for banks and financial institutions to file an application before the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT)?
questions.explanation: The Central Government increased the minimum debt threshold for filing recovery applications before DRT under Section 1(4) of the RDB Act from Rs. 10 Lakhs to Rs. 20 Lakhs in 2018.

questions.question: Under Section 211 and 212 of Companies Act 2013, the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) can initiate investigation into affairs of a company only on:
questions.option_a: A police complaint filed by an operational creditor
questions.option_b: An order of the Central Government (Ministry of Corporate Affairs) based on registrar report, special resolution, or public interest
questions.option_c: A unilateral request by the Resolution Professional
questions.option_d: An ex-parte application before the High Court
questions.explanation: Under Section 212(1) of Companies Act 2013, SFIO investigates upon an order of the Central Government if it is of opinion that it is necessary to investigate into company affairs on report of registrar/inspector, special resolution, or in public interest.

questions.question: Under the proviso to Section 31(4) of IBC, where a resolution plan contains a combination as per Section 5 of Competition Act 2002, when must the approval of CCI be obtained?
questions.option_b: Prior to the approval of such resolution plan by the Committee of Creditors
questions.option_c: Only after the resolution applicant pays all financial creditors
questions.option_d: CCI approval is completely exempt for IBC resolution plans
questions.explanation: The proviso to Section 31(4) of IBC requires that where the resolution plan contains a combination, the resolution applicant shall obtain the approval of the Competition Commission of India prior to the approval of the resolution plan by the CoC.

questions.question: Under Section 79 of the Income Tax Act 1961, carry forward and set off of losses is not allowed if 51% voting power changes. How does this apply to companies undergoing CIRP?
questions.option_a: Section 79 completely denies loss carry-forward to all resolution applicants
questions.option_b: Section 79(2)(c) exempts companies where change in shareholding takes place pursuant to an approved resolution plan under IBC after giving opportunity of being heard to the jurisdictional Principal Commissioner
questions.option_c: Losses can only be carried forward for a maximum of 1 year
questions.option_d: Tax losses are written off 100% on insolvency commencement
questions.explanation: Section 79(2)(c) of the Income Tax Act provides an explicit carve-out for corporate debtors undergoing CIRP under IBC, allowing carry-forward of business losses despite change in 51% shareholding pursuant to an approved plan.

questions.question: Under Indian Stamp Act 1899, what is the legal consequence of an instrument chargeable with duty not being duly stamped?
questions.option_a: The document is completely criminal and punishable with imprisonment
questions.option_b: It shall not be admissible in evidence for any purpose, nor acted upon, registered or authenticated, until duty and penalty are paid
questions.option_c: It remains fully enforceable before civil courts without penalty
questions.option_d: It becomes valid automatically after 3 years
questions.explanation: Section 35 of the Indian Stamp Act provides that no instrument chargeable with duty shall be admitted in evidence for any purpose, or acted upon, unless such instrument is duly stamped, subject to payment of deficit duty and penalty.

questions.question: Under the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA) 1999 and RBI regulations, can an overseas resolution applicant acquire equity shares of an Indian corporate debtor under an approved resolution plan?
questions.option_a: No, foreign investment in distressed companies is prohibited
questions.option_b: Yes, subject to sectoral caps and FDI pricing guidelines/approvals as applicable under the FEMA (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules
questions.option_c: Only if the overseas entity pays in gold bullion
questions.option_d: Only with prior sanction of the President of India
questions.explanation: Overseas resolution applicants can acquire shares of Indian corporate debtors under IBC resolution plans subject to compliance with the sectoral caps, entry routes, and reporting requirements under FEMA (NDI) Rules, 2019.

questions.question: Under the IBBI (CIRP) Regulations, what is the definition of "Fair Value"?
questions.option_a: The historical cost of assets as recorded in the audited balance sheet
questions.option_b: The estimated realizable value of the assets if the corporate debtor were to be liquidated on insolvency commencement date
questions.option_c: The estimated realizable value of the assets at which an asset may be exchanged between a willing buyer and a willing seller in an arm’s length transaction after proper marketing
questions.option_d: The replacement cost of all machinery minus 20% depreciation
questions.explanation: Regulation 2(1)(hb) of CIRP Regulations defines "fair value" as the estimated realizable value of the assets of the corporate debtor at which they may be exchanged between a willing buyer and a willing seller on the insolvency commencement date.

questions.question: What is the definition of "Liquidation Value" under Regulation 2(1)(k) of IBBI (CIRP) Regulations?
questions.option_a: The book value of all current assets plus investments
questions.option_b: The estimated realizable value of the assets of the corporate debtor if the corporate debtor were to be liquidated on the insolvency commencement date
questions.option_c: The price quoted on stock exchanges on insolvency commencement date
questions.option_d: The market value of land and buildings alone
questions.explanation: Regulation 2(1)(k) defines "liquidation value" as the estimated realizable value of the assets of the corporate debtor if the corporate debtor were to be liquidated on the insolvency commencement date.

questions.question: Which financial metric indicates whether a company generates enough cash from operations to cover its annual debt interest expenses?
questions.explanation: Interest Coverage Ratio measures how easily a company can pay interest on its outstanding debt with operating profits: ICR = EBIT / Interest Expense. A ratio below 1 indicates insolvency risk.

questions.question: In corporate debt restructuring, what is "Haircut" in financial parlance?
questions.option_a: The administrative fee deducted by the Resolution Professional
questions.option_b: The percentage reduction or write-off in the claim value accepted by creditors under a resolution plan compared to their total outstanding debt
questions.option_c: The statutory TDS deducted on bank interest
questions.option_d: The legal stamp duty charged by state governments
questions.explanation: A haircut represents the percentage sacrifice or write-off accepted by lenders/creditors on their total admitted claims to make a corporate turnaround viable under a resolution plan.

questions.question: Under Ind AS 1 (Presentation of Financial Statements), when the management or IRP determines that the company has no realistic alternative but to cease trading or liquidate, financial statements must NOT be prepared on:
questions.explanation: Ind AS 1 requires financial statements to be prepared on a going concern basis unless management intends to liquidate the entity or cease operations, in which case the going concern assumption is invalid.

questions.question: If a Corporate Debtor has Current Assets of Rs. 120 Crore and Current Liabilities of Rs. 160 Crore, what is its Current Ratio and Working Capital status?
questions.option_a: Current Ratio 0.75:1 with Negative Working Capital of Rs. 40 Crore
questions.option_b: Current Ratio 1.33:1 with Positive Working Capital of Rs. 40 Crore
questions.explanation: Current Ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities = 120 / 160 = 0.75. Working Capital = CA - CL = 120 - 160 = -Rs. 40 Crore (Net deficit/negative working capital).

questions.question: Under Section 188 of the IBC, the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) consists of a Chairperson and how many members?
questions.option_a: Three whole-time members and two part-time members
questions.option_b: Ten members including Chairperson, three members from Central Government ministries (Finance, Corporate Affairs, Law), one nominee of RBI, and up to five other members nominated by Central Government
questions.option_c: Five members all appointed by the Chief Justice of India
questions.option_d: Only the Chairperson and a Registrar
questions.explanation: Section 188(1) provides that IBBI consists of a Chairperson, three members from Central Government ministries, one member nominated by RBI, and up to five other members nominated by the Central Government.

questions.question: What is the primary role of an Information Utility (IU) under Section 209-216 of the IBC 2016?
questions.option_a: To adjudicate admission of Section 7 and 9 applications
questions.option_b: To collect, collate, authenticate and disseminate financial information to facilitate swift establishment of defaults
questions.option_c: To hold physical custody of mortgaged factory assets
questions.option_d: To conduct e-auctions of corporate debtor assets during liquidation
questions.explanation: Information Utilities (such as NeSL) collect, authenticate and store financial information, and generate records of default which serve as indisputable evidence for NCLT to admit Section 7 petitions.

questions.question: By the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Act 2020, what threshold was introduced under Section 7 proviso for allottees under a real estate project to file a CIRP application?
questions.option_a: Any single homebuyer with dues exceeding Rs. 1 Lakh
questions.option_b: Jointly by not less than 100 of such allottees or not less than 10% of the total number of allottees under the same real estate project, whichever is less
questions.option_c: At least 51% of all registered homebuyers in value
questions.option_d: Only the registered RERA Resident Welfare Association (RWA)
questions.explanation: Section 7(1) second proviso mandates that for real estate allottees, the application must be filed jointly by not less than 100 allottees or not less than 10% of total allottees under the same project, whichever is less (upheld in Manish Kumar v. UOI).

questions.question: According to IBBI publications and the BLRC report, what was the paramount legislative objective behind enacting the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016?
questions.option_a: Recovery of loans for public sector banks at all costs
questions.option_b: Reorganization and insolvency resolution of corporate persons, partnership firms and individuals in a time bound manner for maximization of value of assets and promoting entrepreneurship
questions.option_c: Direct liquidation of defaulting companies within 30 days
questions.explanation: The Preamble of IBC 2016 states its paramount objectives: reorganization and insolvency resolution in a time-bound manner, maximization of value of assets, promotion of entrepreneurship, and balancing the interests of all stakeholders.

questions.question: Who acts as the "Appellate Authority" against the orders of the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) in insolvency matters under Section 61 of IBC?
questions.option_a: High Court of the respective state
questions.option_d: Governor of Reserve Bank of India
questions.explanation: Section 61(1) provides that any person aggrieved by an order of the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) under Part II may prefer an appeal to the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT).

questions.question: Case Study: Alpha Infra Ltd. is in CIRP with admitted financial debt of Rs. 500 Cr (Consortium of 4 banks) and operational debt of Rs. 80 Cr. Two resolution plans were received: Plan A offering Rs. 350 Cr upfront, and Plan B offering Rs. 320 Cr over 2 years. 70% of CoC votes in favor of Plan A. The dissenting 30% financial creditors argue they should get immediate cash equal to liquidation value. Under Section 30(2)(b), what are the dissenting financial creditors entitled to receive?
questions.option_a: Nothing, as the majority decision binds everyone without condition
questions.option_b: An amount not less than the amount to be paid to such creditors in accordance with sub-section (1) of section 53 in the event of a liquidation of the corporate debtor
questions.option_c: 100% of their total financial claim in cash on day 1
questions.option_d: Equity shares in the resolution applicant company
questions.explanation: Section 30(2)(b)(ii) guarantees that dissenting financial creditors must receive an amount not less than the amount that would have been paid to them under Section 53(1) in the event of a liquidation.

questions.question: Case Study: In the liquidation of Zenith Motors Ltd., total liquidation estate realized is Rs. 150 Crore. The claims admitted are: CIRP and Liquidation costs: Rs. 10 Cr; Workmen dues (last 24 months): Rs. 20 Cr; Secured Financial Creditors with relinquished security: Rs. 100 Cr; Unsecured Financial Creditors: Rs. 40 Cr; Central Excise & GST dues (preceding 2 years): Rs. 15 Cr. What amount will Secured Financial Creditors and Workmen receive under Section 53(1)(b)?
questions.option_a: Workmen get Rs. 20 Cr in full, Secured Creditors get Rs. 100 Cr in full
questions.option_b: After Rs. 10 Cr liquidation costs, the remaining Rs. 140 Cr is shared between Secured Creditors (Rs. 100 Cr) and Workmen (Rs. 20 Cr) pari passu, so both are paid 100% (total Rs. 120 Cr)
questions.option_c: Secured creditors get Rs. 140 Cr and workmen get nothing
questions.option_d: All creditors receive an equal 20% dividend
questions.explanation: Under Section 53(1)(a), CIRP/Liquidation costs (Rs. 10 Cr) are paid first, leaving Rs. 140 Cr. Under Section 53(1)(b), workmen dues (24 months = Rs. 20 Cr) and secured creditors (Rs. 100 Cr) rank equally (pari passu). Since Rs. 120 Cr <= Rs. 140 Cr available, both are paid in full (Rs. 120 Cr total), leaving Rs. 20 Cr for unsecured financial creditors under 53(1)(d).

questions.question: Case Study: Six months before insolvency commencement date, the Managing Director of Beta Polymers Ltd. caused the company to transfer 5 commercial trucks worth Rs. 1.2 Crore to his brother-in-law’s proprietary firm for a recorded price of Rs. 20 Lakhs. The Resolution Professional discovers this during CIRP. Under which provisions should the RP file an application before NCLT?
questions.option_b: Section 45 (Undervalued Transactions) and Section 66 (Fraudulent Trading / Transactions defrauding creditors)
questions.option_d: Section 186 of Companies Act 2013 before High Court
questions.explanation: The transfer of assets worth Rs. 1.2 Cr for Rs. 20 Lakhs to a related party is an Undervalued Transaction under Section 45 (look-back 2 years) and also constitutes Fraudulent Trading / defrauding creditors under Section 66 of IBC.

questions.question: Case Study: MicroTech Components (an MSME corporate debtor) initiates PPIRP under Section 54A. The promoters submit a Base Resolution Plan providing for 65% payment to financial creditors and 100% to operational creditors, but impairing some claims. The CoC requires the promoters to compete against third-party resolution applicants. Under Section 54K(4), if the base plan impairs debts owed to operational creditors, what must the CoC require?
questions.option_a: Immediate rejection of PPIRP and conversion to liquidation
questions.option_b: The RP must invite prospective resolution applicants to submit competing resolution plans against the base resolution plan (Swiss Challenge mechanism)
questions.option_c: The promoters must pay operational creditors from their personal provident fund within 24 hours
questions.option_d: Adjudicating Authority approval without any voting
questions.explanation: Under Section 54K(4) of IBC, where the base resolution plan does not provide for payment to operational creditors of the amount not less than liquidation value, or impairs operational debt, CoC must require the RP to invite competing resolution plans (Swiss Challenge).

questions.question:
[Case Study: CIRP of Sunrise Steel Ltd.]
On admission of the Section 7 application on 1 March 2024, what is the "insolvency commencement date"?
questions.explanation: Section 5(12) of IBC defines "insolvency commencement date" as the date of admission of the application under Sections 7, 9 or 10 by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT). It is 1 March 2024.

questions.question:
[Case Study: CIRP of Sunrise Steel Ltd.]
After Mr. Ravi Sharma is appointed as IRP, what happens to the Board of Directors of SSL?
questions.option_a: Board continues to function under IRP supervision
questions.option_c: Board is suspended and powers vest in IRP
questions.option_d: Board is asked to resign within 7 days
questions.explanation: Section 17 of IBC: On insolvency commencement date, management of corporate debtor vests in IRP and Board of Directors stands suspended. IRP takes over management of the corporate debtor.

questions.question:
[Case Study: CIRP of Sunrise Steel Ltd.]
Mr. Ravi Sharma must constitute the Committee of Creditors (CoC). Who will be members of the CoC?
questions.option_a: National Bank and City Bank only
questions.option_b: National Bank, City Bank and ABC Suppliers
questions.option_d: Only National Bank as it has the largest claim
questions.explanation: Section 21 of IBC: CoC shall comprise all financial creditors. Operational creditors are NOT members of CoC unless there are no financial creditors. National Bank (Rs. 200 Cr) and City Bank (Rs. 50 Cr) are financial creditors. ABC Suppliers is an operational creditor and will not be part of CoC.

questions.question:
[Case Study: CIRP of Sunrise Steel Ltd.]
The CoC resolves to extend CIRP by 90 days. The voting requirement for this resolution is:
questions.explanation: Section 12(2) of IBC: The resolution for extension of CIRP period requires approval of CoC by a vote of 66% of voting shares. The voting share of each financial creditor is in proportion to their financial debt.

questions.question:
[Case Study: Liquidation of Phoenix Textiles Ltd.]
What is the total realisation available for distribution (assuming all assets are sold at stated values)?
questions.explanation: Total assets = Factory (80) + Machinery (20) + Stock/Receivables (15) = Rs. 115 Crore. This is the total liquidation estate available for distribution.

questions.question:
[Case Study: Liquidation of Phoenix Textiles Ltd.]
After paying CIRP costs of Rs. 3 Crore and workmen/employee dues of Rs. 5 Crore, how much is available for National Bank (secured creditor)?
questions.explanation: Section 53 waterfall: Step 1 — CIRP costs Rs. 3 Cr. Step 2 — Workmen (24 months) Rs. 5 Cr. After these two: 115 - 3 - 5 = Rs. 107 Cr available. National Bank as secured creditor ranks next and gets up to Rs. 90 Cr (their claim), leaving Rs. 17 Cr.

questions.question:
[Case Study: Liquidation of Phoenix Textiles Ltd.]
National Bank relinquished its security to the liquidation estate. After paying CIRP costs and workmen dues, in the Section 53 waterfall, unsecured operational creditors will receive:
questions.explanation: After CIRP costs (3) + workmen dues (5) + National Bank secured (90) + Government dues (4) = 102 Cr. Remaining = 115 - 102 = 13 Cr. Operational creditors get Rs. 13 Cr on pro-rata against their Rs. 25 Cr claim. (Note: Employee dues beyond 24 months and remaining secured creditor claims would also need consideration — simplified here.)

questions.question:
[Case Study: Pre-Pack of TechSolutions Pvt Ltd (MSME)]
Is TechSolutions Pvt Ltd eligible for Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process?
questions.option_a: Yes, as it is an MSME
questions.option_b: No, as default amount is above threshold
questions.option_c: No, only listed companies are eligible
questions.explanation: Chapter III-A of IBC (Sections 54A-54P) provides for PPIRP only for MSMEs (Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises) as defined under the MSMED Act 2006. TechSolutions qualifies as an MSME.

questions.question:
[Case Study: Pre-Pack of TechSolutions Pvt Ltd (MSME)]
Under Pre-Pack process, when must the base resolution plan be submitted?
questions.option_d: At the time of plan approval
