questions.explanation: Under Pre-Pack Regulations, the prospective resolution applicant must submit the base resolution plan along with the Section 7 application filed by the financial creditor before NCLT.

questions.question:
[Case Study: Pre-Pack of TechSolutions Pvt Ltd (MSME)]
If the CoC rejects the base resolution plan under Pre-Pack, what happens?
questions.option_b: New resolution applicants can submit plans
questions.option_d: Process restarts with new base plan
questions.explanation: Under PPIRP, if CoC rejects the base plan, the process converts to regular CIRP and other resolution applicants can submit resolution plans. The base plan applicant gets certain advantages but not exclusivity.

questions.question:
[Case Study: Pre-Pack of TechSolutions Pvt Ltd (MSME)]
What is the timeline for completing Pre-Pack process for MSMEs?
questions.explanation: For MSMEs, the Pre-Pack process must be completed within 90 days from the insolvency commencement date. This is shorter than the regular CIRP timeline of 180 days extendable to 270 days.

questions.question:
[Case Study: Individual Insolvency of Mr. Rajesh Kumar]
Which process under IBC Part III is available to Mr. Rajesh Kumar given his debt level and assets?
questions.explanation: Given his debt level (Rs. 25 Lakhs) and asset value (Rs. 8 Lakhs), Mr. Rajesh Kumar would likely qualify for the Fresh Start Process if thresholds are met. The exact thresholds are prescribed by the government but Fresh Start is for lower debt/assets cases.

questions.question:
[Case Study: Individual Insolvency of Mr. Rajesh Kumar]
Under the Fresh Start Process, what happens to Mr. Rajesh Kumar's residential property?
questions.option_a: It will be sold to repay debts
questions.option_b: It may be exempt up to a certain value
questions.option_c: It automatically becomes property of the trustee
questions.option_d: He can retain it without conditions
questions.explanation: Under Fresh Start Process, certain essential assets including residential property up to a prescribed value may be exempt from liquidation, allowing the debtor a fresh start while creditors receive partial payment from other assets.

questions.question:
[Case Study: Individual Insolvency of Mr. Rajesh Kumar]
If Mr. Rajesh Kumar completes the Fresh Start Process successfully, what is the status of his remaining debts?
questions.option_b: Debts are restructured and he must pay
questions.option_c: He remains liable for all debts
questions.explanation: Upon successful completion of Fresh Start Process, the debtor receives a discharge from all qualifying debts, giving them a fresh start. This is similar to bankruptcy discharge in other jurisdictions.

questions.question:
[Case Study: Individual Insolvency of Mr. Rajesh Kumar]
What is the role of the Insolvency Professional in individual insolvency under IBC?
questions.option_b: Evaluate the debtor's assets and liabilities
questions.explanation: The Insolvency Professional (or trustee as the case may be) in individual insolvency manages the process, evaluates assets and liabilities, and distributes proceeds to creditors according to the prescribed waterfall for individuals.

questions.question:
[Case Study: Power Purchase Agreement Termination - Energy Corp]
Under the Gujarat Urja v. Amit Gupta principle, when does contract termination violate moratorium?
questions.option_b: Termination solely on grounds of insolvency
questions.explanation: As per Gujarat Urja case, termination of contracts solely on grounds of insolvency (ipso facto clauses) violates moratorium under Section 14(1)(d). Termination for valid commercial reasons (not solely insolvency) may be permitted.

questions.question:
[Case Study: Power Purchase Agreement Termination - Energy Corp]
Is the PPA a financial contract that would fall under the exception to moratorium under Section 14(2A)?
questions.option_a: Yes, all PPAs are financial contracts
questions.option_b: No, PPA is not a financial contract
questions.explanation: A Power Purchase Agreement is typically not a financial contract under Section 14(2A). Financial contracts generally include securities, derivatives, repo transactions, etc. PPAs are commercial contracts and termination solely for insolvency would violate moratorium.

questions.question:
[Case Study: Power Purchase Agreement Termination - Energy Corp]
If the SEB cannot terminate the PPA, what are Energy Corp's obligations under the agreement?
questions.option_a: All obligations are suspended during CIRP
questions.option_b: Energy Corp must continue performing if it can
questions.option_c: SEB must continue buying power at agreed rates
questions.explanation: Under moratorium, the corporate debtor's obligations continue if performance is possible. The counterparty cannot terminate solely due to insolvency but the debtor must perform if it has the means. The rights and obligations are modified but not extinguished.

questions.question:
[Case Study: Power Purchase Agreement Termination - Energy Corp]
What happens if the termination was indeed for payment default (not solely insolvency)?
questions.option_b: It would be permitted under IBC
questions.option_c: NCLT would decide based on facts
questions.explanation: If termination is for actual payment default and not solely due to insolvency status, the analysis changes. NCLT would examine the facts to determine if the termination is ipso facto (solely insolvency-based) or based on legitimate commercial grounds. The Gujarat Urja distinction is critical.

questions.question:
[Case Study: Contract Dispute During CIRP - BuildCorp Ltd]
The contract clause "terminates if either party becomes insolvent" is known as:
questions.explanation: An ipso facto clause is a contract provision that allows termination or modification of the contract upon occurrence of insolvency or bankruptcy proceedings. Such clauses are generally ineffective under IBC moratorium.

questions.question:
[Case Study: Contract Dispute During CIRP - BuildCorp Ltd]
Under Indian Contract Act, when does an agreement become void?
questions.option_a: When it is against public policy
questions.option_b: When it is prohibited by law
questions.explanation: Under Section 23 of Indian Contract Act, agreements are void if they are against public policy, prohibited by law, involve fraud/misrepresentation, or if parties lack capacity (minors, persons of unsound mind). An ipso facto clause may be void under IBC even if valid under Contract Act.

questions.question:
[Case Study: Contract Dispute During CIRP - BuildCorp Ltd]
How does the principle in Gujarat Urja apply to this contract termination?
questions.option_c: It does not apply to commercial contracts
questions.explanation: Gujarat Urja principle applies to contract termination solely on grounds of insolvency. The clause allowing termination "if either party becomes insolvent" is a classic ipso facto clause and would be ineffective under IBC moratorium.

questions.question:
[Case Study: Contract Dispute During CIRP - BuildCorp Ltd]
What remedies does the RP have against Supplier X for wrongful termination?
questions.option_a: Claim damages for breach of contract
questions.option_d: No remedy as contract is void
questions.explanation: The RP can seek remedies for wrongful termination that violates moratorium. This may include damages for breach of contract or seeking specific performance if the contract is essential for the corporate debtor's revival.

case_laws.case_name: Committee of Creditors of Essar Steel India Ltd. v. Satish Kumar Gupta
case_laws.facts: Essar Steel underwent CIRP. The NCLAT modified the resolution plan approved by CoC by directing equal treatment of all financial and operational creditors. The resolution plan was challenged.
case_laws.issue: Whether NCLAT can modify a resolution plan approved by CoC? What is the binding nature of CoC decisions? Whether secured financial creditors can be differentiated from operational creditors?
case_laws.judgment: Supreme Court held: (1) CoC has commercial wisdom to decide distribution in resolution plan. (2) NCLAT cannot modify commercial decisions of CoC. (3) Differentiation between financial and operational creditors is valid. (4) Resolution plan must provide for payment of at least liquidation value to dissenting creditors.
case_laws.outcome: NCLAT order set aside. Resolution plan as approved by CoC restored.
case_laws.exam_principle: CoC's commercial wisdom is paramount. Courts cannot substitute their judgment for CoC's commercial decisions. Secured financial creditors can be differentiated from operational creditors in a resolution plan.

case_laws.case_name: Swiss Ribbons Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India
case_laws.facts: Constitutional validity of IBC was challenged on grounds of discrimination between financial and operational creditors, arbitrary powers to IBBI, etc.
case_laws.issue: Whether IBC is constitutionally valid? Whether differentiation between financial and operational creditors is arbitrary?
case_laws.provisions: Articles 14, 19(1)(g) of Constitution; Sections 7, 8, 9, 21, 24, 25, 28, 30 of IBC
case_laws.judgment: Supreme Court upheld constitutional validity of IBC. Held: (1) IBC is not a recovery law but a resolution law. (2) Differentiation between financial and operational creditors is intelligible differentia with rational nexus to object. (3) IBBI has quasi-judicial powers. (4) IBC aims at revival of company as going concern.
case_laws.exam_principle: IBC is a complete code for resolution, not merely a recovery mechanism. Differentiation between creditors is constitutionally valid. The primary objective is maximisation of value of assets.

case_laws.case_name: Mobilox Innovations Pvt. Ltd. v. Kirusa Software Pvt. Ltd.
case_laws.facts: Kirusa filed an application under Section 9 against Mobilox for unpaid operational dues. Mobilox raised a dispute about quality of services. NCLT admitted the application. NCLAT affirmed.
case_laws.issue: What constitutes a "dispute" under Section 8(2)(a) of IBC to defeat an operational creditor's application under Section 9?
case_laws.judgment: SC held: A "pre-existing dispute" must exist before the demand notice under Section 8. The word "dispute" includes any bona fide dispute raised. NCLT is not required to examine merits of dispute — only whether a plausible dispute exists.
case_laws.exam_principle: Under Section 9, NCLT must be satisfied that there is NO pre-existing dispute before admitting the application. The existence of a bona fide pre-existing dispute is a complete defence to a Section 9 application.

case_laws.case_name: Arcelormittal India Pvt. Ltd. v. Satish Kumar Gupta
case_laws.facts: Question arose whether persons who were promoters/directors of NPA companies were eligible to be resolution applicants under IBC.
case_laws.issue: Whether Section 29A of IBC (eligibility criteria for resolution applicants) is constitutionally valid? Who is disqualified from submitting resolution plan?
case_laws.judgment: SC upheld Section 29A as constitutional. Held: (1) Promoters/connected persons who pushed the company into insolvency cannot be allowed to buy it back at a discount through IRP process. (2) "Control" under Section 29A(c) must be read broadly. (3) The provision prevents persons who contributed to corporate debtor's insolvency from benefiting.
case_laws.outcome: Section 29A upheld. Certain resolution applicants held ineligible.
case_laws.exam_principle: Section 29A bars willful defaulters, undischarged insolvents, persons convicted of certain offences, and persons connected to NPA accounts from being resolution applicants. Protects IBC from misuse by erstwhile promoters.

case_laws.case_name: Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank
case_laws.facts: First major IBC case. ICICI Bank filed Section 7 application against Innoventive Industries. Corporate debtor contended that Maharashtra Relief Undertakings Act protected it from insolvency proceedings.
case_laws.issue: Whether IBC overrides state laws? What is the nature of NCLT's jurisdiction under Section 7?
case_laws.provisions: Sections 7, 14 of IBC; Article 254 of Constitution
case_laws.judgment: SC held: (1) IBC overrides all state enactments by repugnancy under Article 254. (2) NCLT must admit Section 7 application if satisfied that: (a) applicant is a financial creditor, (b) a debt exists, (c) a default has occurred. (3) NCLT cannot go behind a default once established.
case_laws.outcome: Section 7 application admitted. State law protection rejected.
case_laws.exam_principle: IBC is a central law and overrides state laws. Once default is established, NCLT must admit Section 7 application — no discretion. Moratorium under Section 14 has overriding effect.

case_laws.case_name: K. Sashidhar v. Indian Overseas Bank
case_laws.facts: Resolution plan was rejected by CoC with 75% voting (before amendment reducing threshold to 66%). Question arose whether NCLT/NCLAT can approve a plan rejected by CoC.
case_laws.issue: Whether NCLT can approve a resolution plan if CoC has rejected it? What is the scope of judicial review of CoC decisions?
case_laws.judgment: SC held: (1) NCLT and NCLAT have limited jurisdiction to review CoC decisions. (2) If resolution plan is rejected by CoC, tribunal has no jurisdiction to approve it. (3) Liquidation must follow. (4) The adjudicating authority cannot examine the commercial wisdom of CoC.
case_laws.outcome: Plan rejection by CoC upheld. Liquidation ordered.
case_laws.exam_principle: Once CoC rejects a resolution plan, NCLT has no jurisdiction to approve it. Judicial review of CoC decisions is very limited — only on grounds of non-compliance with procedure or law, not commercial merits.

case_laws.case_name: Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Ltd. v. Amit Gupta
case_laws.facts: Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) was terminated by GUVNL on grounds of insolvency-related default. RP challenged the termination claiming it violated the moratorium.
case_laws.issue: Whether termination of contracts solely on grounds of insolvency violates moratorium under Section 14(1)(d)? What is ipso facto clause?
case_laws.judgment: SC held: (1) Termination of contracts solely on the ground of insolvency (ipso facto clauses) violates moratorium. (2) However, Section 14(2A) carves out an exception for financial contracts. (3) Government contracts can be terminated if termination is not ipso facto but for other valid reasons.
case_laws.outcome: PPA termination held invalid as it was solely due to insolvency.
case_laws.exam_principle: Ipso facto clauses — contract termination solely on insolvency — violate moratorium. Contracts cannot be terminated only because of insolvency proceedings. Exception for financial contracts under 14(2A).

case_laws.case_name: Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. v. Spade Financial Services Ltd.
case_laws.facts: Issue related to whether a non-performing asset can be sold at a price less than the fair value determined by valuers.
case_laws.issue: Whether sale of NPA below fair value is permissible? What is the role of registered valuers in asset valuation?
case_laws.provisions: Section 29A, IBC; SARFAESI Act; Regulation 27 of IBBI (CIRP) Regulations
case_laws.judgment: SC held: (1) Sale of NPA below fair value is permissible if it is the best possible offer. (2) Fair value is only a reference point, not the floor price. (3) CoC has commercial wisdom to accept the best offer even if below fair value.
case_laws.outcome: Sale of NPA below fair value upheld.
case_laws.exam_principle: Fair value determined by registered valuers is not the minimum price for asset sale. CoC's commercial wisdom prevails in accepting the best offer for maximization of value.

case_laws.case_name: Jindal Steel & Power Ltd. v. National Company Law Tribunal
case_laws.facts: Issue regarding the period of limitation for filing application under Section 7 of IBC.
case_laws.issue: What is the limitation period for filing Section 7 application after default?
case_laws.judgment: SC held: (1) For financial creditors, limitation starts from the date of default and not from the date of demand notice. (2) If the debt is a time-barred debt, Section 7 application cannot be filed. (3) Financial debt must be established along with default.
case_laws.exam_principle: Section 7 application must be filed within the limitation period from the date of default. Time-barred debts cannot be the basis for CIRP application.

case_laws.case_name: V. Padmakumar v. Stressed Assets Stabilisation Fund
case_laws.facts: Issue regarding immunity from civil proceedings against the Resolution Professional.
case_laws.issue: Whether RP has immunity from civil proceedings for actions taken in good faith during CIRP?
case_laws.provisions: Section 234 of IBC; Regulation 6 of IBBI (IP) Regulations
case_laws.judgment: SC held: (1) RP has immunity from civil proceedings for actions taken in good faith in discharge of duties. (2) This immunity is not absolute and does not extend to fraudulent or malicious acts. (3) The immunity is necessary for effective functioning of CIRP.
case_laws.outcome: RP granted immunity for actions taken in good faith.
case_laws.exam_principle: Resolution Professionals have immunity from civil suits for actions taken in good faith during CIRP. This immunity is necessary for effective implementation of IBC.

case_laws.case_name: MBR Infrastructures Ltd. v. Tata Steel Ltd.
case_laws.facts: Issue regarding whether CoC can reject all resolution plans and direct liquidation.
case_laws.issue: Whether CoC can reject all resolution plans and opt for liquidation?
case_laws.judgment: NCLAT held: (1) CoC has the commercial wisdom to reject all resolution plans. (2) If CoC rejects all plans, liquidation follows as per Section 33. (3) NCLT cannot force CoC to accept a resolution plan.
case_laws.outcome: CoC decision to reject all plans upheld.
case_laws.exam_principle: CoC has the commercial wisdom to reject all resolution plans. Liquidation is the inevitable consequence if no acceptable resolution plan is received.

case_laws.case_name: Pioneer Polyleathers Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India
case_laws.facts: Issue regarding whether operational creditors can be part of CoC.
case_laws.issue: Whether operational creditors can be members of Committee of Creditors?
case_laws.judgment: SC held: (1) Operational creditors are not members of CoC under Section 21. (2) They can only participate in meetings if CoC decides. (3) This distinction is constitutionally valid as upheld in Swiss Ribbons.
case_laws.outcome: Operational creditors held not to be CoC members.
case_laws.exam_principle: Operational creditors are not members of CoC unless there are no financial creditors. They have limited participation rights in CIRP.

case_laws.facts: Issue regarding disciplinary proceedings against Insolvency Professional.
case_laws.issue: Whether IBBI can initiate disciplinary proceedings against IP for misconduct?
case_laws.judgment: NCLAT held: (1) IBBI has power to initiate disciplinary proceedings against IPs for misconduct. (2) The procedure must be fair and natural justice must be followed. (3) Penalties can include suspension or cancellation of registration.
case_laws.exam_principle: IBBI has disciplinary jurisdiction over Insolvency Professionals. IPs must adhere to the Code of Conduct and can face penalties for misconduct.

case_laws.case_name: Binani Industries Ltd. v. Bank of Baroda
case_laws.facts: Issue regarding whether CoC can extend CIRP period beyond statutory limits.
case_laws.issue: Whether CoC can extend CIRP beyond 270 days?
case_laws.judgment: NCLAT held: (1) CIRP period is 180 days extendable by 90 days (total 270 days). (2) CoC cannot extend beyond statutory limits. (3) Extension beyond 270 days requires NCLT approval under exceptional circumstances.
case_laws.outcome: Extension beyond 270 days without NCLT approval not allowed.
case_laws.exam_principle: CIRP timeline is statutorily fixed at 180+90 days. CoC cannot extend beyond this without NCLT approval in exceptional circumstances.

case_laws.facts: Issue regarding homebuyers as financial creditors and resolution plan for real estate projects.
case_laws.issue: Whether homebuyers are financial creditors? Can resolution plan include completion of unfinished projects?
case_laws.provisions: Section 5(8)(f) of IBC; Section 30 of IBC
case_laws.judgment: SC held: (1) Homebuyers are financial creditors under Section 5(8)(f). (2) Resolution plan can include completion of unfinished real estate projects. (3) Maximum value for homebuyers can be the amount paid or actual cost of apartment, whichever is higher.
case_laws.exam_principle: Homebuyers are financial creditors under IBC. Resolution plans for real estate companies can include project completion as part of the resolution strategy.

case_laws.case_name: Ruchi Soya Industries Ltd. v. Patanjali Ayurved Ltd.
case_laws.facts: Issue regarding eligibility of resolution applicant with non-performing assets.
case_laws.issue: Whether a resolution applicant with NPAs in other companies is eligible under Section 29A?
case_laws.judgment: NCLAT held: (1) Section 29A disqualifies resolution applicants with NPAs. (2) The disqualification applies to the applicant and related parties. (3) However, NPA must be subsisting as on the date of application.
case_laws.outcome: Resolution applicant held ineligible due to NPA.
case_laws.exam_principle: Section 29A disqualifies resolution applicants with non-performing assets. This prevents entities that have contributed to insolvency from acquiring stressed assets.

case_studies.title: CIRP of Sunrise Steel Ltd.
case_studies.scenario: Sunrise Steel Ltd. (SSL) is a company incorporated under the Companies Act 2013. SSL took a term loan of Rs. 200 Crore from National Bank (NB) and working capital facilities of Rs. 50 Crore from City Bank (CB). SSL also owes Rs. 10 Crore to ABC Suppliers (an operational creditor) for raw material supply. SSL defaulted on repayment of term loan instalment of Rs. 15 Crore to National Bank on 1 January 2024. National Bank issued a demand notice. SSL did not respond. National Bank filed an application under Section 7 before NCLT on 15 February 2024. NCLT admitted the application on 1 March 2024 and appointed Mr. Ravi Sharma as IRP. SSL has 500 employees and owns a manufacturing plant worth Rs. 300 Crore (as per books) and Rs. 250 Crore (fair value).

case_studies.title: Liquidation of Phoenix Textiles Ltd.
case_studies.scenario: Phoenix Textiles Ltd. (PTL) underwent CIRP. No resolution plan was received within the CIRP period. The NCLT passed a liquidation order on 1 June 2024 and appointed Ms. Priya Mehta as Liquidator. The assets of PTL are: Factory land and building (secured by National Bank) — Rs. 80 Crore; Machinery — Rs. 20 Crore; Stock and receivables — Rs. 15 Crore. CIRP costs: Rs. 3 Crore. National Bank (secured creditor): Rs. 90 Crore claim, security of factory worth Rs. 80 Crore. Employees: 24-month wages due Rs. 5 Crore. Government dues (GST): Rs. 4 Crore. Unsecured operational creditors: Rs. 25 Crore.

case_studies.title: Pre-Pack of TechSolutions Pvt Ltd (MSME)
case_studies.scenario: TechSolutions Pvt Ltd is an MSME (investment in plant and machinery: Rs. 45 Lakhs). It has defaulted on a loan of Rs. 1.5 Crore from ABC Bank. The promoter has found a buyer, Digital Corp, willing to invest Rs. 2 Crore and revive the company. They want to use the Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PPIRP). The promoter approaches ABC Bank with a base resolution plan. ABC Bank files a Section 7 application along with the base resolution plan.

case_studies.title: Individual Insolvency of Mr. Rajesh Kumar
case_studies.scenario: Mr. Rajesh Kumar, a sole proprietor, has taken personal loans totaling Rs. 25 Lakhs from various lenders. His business has failed and he has no assets except a small residential property worth Rs. 8 Lakhs (which is his only residence). He wants to file for insolvency under IBC Part III. His monthly income is Rs. 15,000 from freelance work.

case_studies.title: Power Purchase Agreement Termination - Energy Corp
case_studies.scenario: Energy Corp Ltd is in CIRP. It has a Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) with State Electricity Board (SEB). The SEB terminates the PPA citing Energy Corp's insolvency and default on payments. The RP challenges this termination, arguing it violates the moratorium under Section 14 of IBC. The SEB claims termination is due to default and not solely due to insolvency.

case_studies.title: Contract Dispute During CIRP - BuildCorp Ltd
case_studies.scenario: BuildCorp Ltd is in CIRP. Before CIRP, it had entered into a contract with Supplier X for construction materials. The contract had a clause stating "this contract shall terminate if either party becomes insolvent." Supplier X terminates the contract citing this clause when BuildCorp enters CIRP. The RP challenges this termination.

case_study_questions.question: On admission of the Section 7 application on 1 March 2024, what is the "insolvency commencement date"?
case_study_questions.explanation: Section 5(12) of IBC defines "insolvency commencement date" as the date of admission of the application under Sections 7, 9 or 10 by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT). It is 1 March 2024.

case_study_questions.question: After Mr. Ravi Sharma is appointed as IRP, what happens to the Board of Directors of SSL?
case_study_questions.option_a: Board continues to function under IRP supervision
case_study_questions.option_c: Board is suspended and powers vest in IRP
case_study_questions.option_d: Board is asked to resign within 7 days
case_study_questions.explanation: Section 17 of IBC: On insolvency commencement date, management of corporate debtor vests in IRP and Board of Directors stands suspended. IRP takes over management of the corporate debtor.

case_study_questions.question: Mr. Ravi Sharma must constitute the Committee of Creditors (CoC). Who will be members of the CoC?
case_study_questions.option_a: National Bank and City Bank only
case_study_questions.option_b: National Bank, City Bank and ABC Suppliers
case_study_questions.option_d: Only National Bank as it has the largest claim
case_study_questions.explanation: Section 21 of IBC: CoC shall comprise all financial creditors. Operational creditors are NOT members of CoC unless there are no financial creditors. National Bank (Rs. 200 Cr) and City Bank (Rs. 50 Cr) are financial creditors. ABC Suppliers is an operational creditor and will not be part of CoC.

case_study_questions.question: The CoC resolves to extend CIRP by 90 days. The voting requirement for this resolution is:
case_study_questions.explanation: Section 12(2) of IBC: The resolution for extension of CIRP period requires approval of CoC by a vote of 66% of voting shares. The voting share of each financial creditor is in proportion to their financial debt.

case_study_questions.question: What is the total realisation available for distribution (assuming all assets are sold at stated values)?
case_study_questions.explanation: Total assets = Factory (80) + Machinery (20) + Stock/Receivables (15) = Rs. 115 Crore. This is the total liquidation estate available for distribution.

case_study_questions.question: After paying CIRP costs of Rs. 3 Crore and workmen/employee dues of Rs. 5 Crore, how much is available for National Bank (secured creditor)?
case_study_questions.explanation: Section 53 waterfall: Step 1 — CIRP costs Rs. 3 Cr. Step 2 — Workmen (24 months) Rs. 5 Cr. After these two: 115 - 3 - 5 = Rs. 107 Cr available. National Bank as secured creditor ranks next and gets up to Rs. 90 Cr (their claim), leaving Rs. 17 Cr.

case_study_questions.question: National Bank relinquished its security to the liquidation estate. After paying CIRP costs and workmen dues, in the Section 53 waterfall, unsecured operational creditors will receive:
case_study_questions.explanation: After CIRP costs (3) + workmen dues (5) + National Bank secured (90) + Government dues (4) = 102 Cr. Remaining = 115 - 102 = 13 Cr. Operational creditors get Rs. 13 Cr on pro-rata against their Rs. 25 Cr claim. (Note: Employee dues beyond 24 months and remaining secured creditor claims would also need consideration — simplified here.)

case_study_questions.question: Is TechSolutions Pvt Ltd eligible for Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process?
case_study_questions.option_a: Yes, as it is an MSME
case_study_questions.option_b: No, as default amount is above threshold
case_study_questions.option_c: No, only listed companies are eligible
case_study_questions.explanation: Chapter III-A of IBC (Sections 54A-54P) provides for PPIRP only for MSMEs (Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises) as defined under the MSMED Act 2006. TechSolutions qualifies as an MSME.

case_study_questions.question: Under Pre-Pack process, when must the base resolution plan be submitted?
case_study_questions.option_d: At the time of plan approval
case_study_questions.explanation: Under Pre-Pack Regulations, the prospective resolution applicant must submit the base resolution plan along with the Section 7 application filed by the financial creditor before NCLT.

case_study_questions.question: If the CoC rejects the base resolution plan under Pre-Pack, what happens?
case_study_questions.option_b: New resolution applicants can submit plans
case_study_questions.option_d: Process restarts with new base plan
case_study_questions.explanation: Under PPIRP, if CoC rejects the base plan, the process converts to regular CIRP and other resolution applicants can submit resolution plans. The base plan applicant gets certain advantages but not exclusivity.

case_study_questions.question: What is the timeline for completing Pre-Pack process for MSMEs?
case_study_questions.explanation: For MSMEs, the Pre-Pack process must be completed within 90 days from the insolvency commencement date. This is shorter than the regular CIRP timeline of 180 days extendable to 270 days.

case_study_questions.question: Which process under IBC Part III is available to Mr. Rajesh Kumar given his debt level and assets?
case_study_questions.explanation: Given his debt level (Rs. 25 Lakhs) and asset value (Rs. 8 Lakhs), Mr. Rajesh Kumar would likely qualify for the Fresh Start Process if thresholds are met. The exact thresholds are prescribed by the government but Fresh Start is for lower debt/assets cases.

case_study_questions.question: Under the Fresh Start Process, what happens to Mr. Rajesh Kumar's residential property?
case_study_questions.option_a: It will be sold to repay debts
case_study_questions.option_b: It may be exempt up to a certain value
case_study_questions.option_c: It automatically becomes property of the trustee
case_study_questions.option_d: He can retain it without conditions
case_study_questions.explanation: Under Fresh Start Process, certain essential assets including residential property up to a prescribed value may be exempt from liquidation, allowing the debtor a fresh start while creditors receive partial payment from other assets.

case_study_questions.question: If Mr. Rajesh Kumar completes the Fresh Start Process successfully, what is the status of his remaining debts?
case_study_questions.option_b: Debts are restructured and he must pay
case_study_questions.option_c: He remains liable for all debts
case_study_questions.explanation: Upon successful completion of Fresh Start Process, the debtor receives a discharge from all qualifying debts, giving them a fresh start. This is similar to bankruptcy discharge in other jurisdictions.

case_study_questions.question: What is the role of the Insolvency Professional in individual insolvency under IBC?
case_study_questions.option_b: Evaluate the debtor's assets and liabilities
case_study_questions.explanation: The Insolvency Professional (or trustee as the case may be) in individual insolvency manages the process, evaluates assets and liabilities, and distributes proceeds to creditors according to the prescribed waterfall for individuals.

case_study_questions.question: Under the Gujarat Urja v. Amit Gupta principle, when does contract termination violate moratorium?
case_study_questions.option_b: Termination solely on grounds of insolvency
case_study_questions.explanation: As per Gujarat Urja case, termination of contracts solely on grounds of insolvency (ipso facto clauses) violates moratorium under Section 14(1)(d). Termination for valid commercial reasons (not solely insolvency) may be permitted.

case_study_questions.question: Is the PPA a financial contract that would fall under the exception to moratorium under Section 14(2A)?
case_study_questions.option_a: Yes, all PPAs are financial contracts
case_study_questions.option_b: No, PPA is not a financial contract
case_study_questions.explanation: A Power Purchase Agreement is typically not a financial contract under Section 14(2A). Financial contracts generally include securities, derivatives, repo transactions, etc. PPAs are commercial contracts and termination solely for insolvency would violate moratorium.

case_study_questions.question: If the SEB cannot terminate the PPA, what are Energy Corp's obligations under the agreement?
case_study_questions.option_a: All obligations are suspended during CIRP
case_study_questions.option_b: Energy Corp must continue performing if it can
case_study_questions.option_c: SEB must continue buying power at agreed rates
case_study_questions.explanation: Under moratorium, the corporate debtor's obligations continue if performance is possible. The counterparty cannot terminate solely due to insolvency but the debtor must perform if it has the means. The rights and obligations are modified but not extinguished.

case_study_questions.question: What happens if the termination was indeed for payment default (not solely insolvency)?
case_study_questions.option_b: It would be permitted under IBC
case_study_questions.option_c: NCLT would decide based on facts
case_study_questions.explanation: If termination is for actual payment default and not solely due to insolvency status, the analysis changes. NCLT would examine the facts to determine if the termination is ipso facto (solely insolvency-based) or based on legitimate commercial grounds. The Gujarat Urja distinction is critical.

case_study_questions.question: The contract clause "terminates if either party becomes insolvent" is known as:
case_study_questions.explanation: An ipso facto clause is a contract provision that allows termination or modification of the contract upon occurrence of insolvency or bankruptcy proceedings. Such clauses are generally ineffective under IBC moratorium.

case_study_questions.question: Under Indian Contract Act, when does an agreement become void?
case_study_questions.option_a: When it is against public policy
case_study_questions.option_b: When it is prohibited by law
case_study_questions.explanation: Under Section 23 of Indian Contract Act, agreements are void if they are against public policy, prohibited by law, involve fraud/misrepresentation, or if parties lack capacity (minors, persons of unsound mind). An ipso facto clause may be void under IBC even if valid under Contract Act.

case_study_questions.question: How does the principle in Gujarat Urja apply to this contract termination?
case_study_questions.option_c: It does not apply to commercial contracts
case_study_questions.explanation: Gujarat Urja principle applies to contract termination solely on grounds of insolvency. The clause allowing termination "if either party becomes insolvent" is a classic ipso facto clause and would be ineffective under IBC moratorium.

case_study_questions.question: What remedies does the RP have against Supplier X for wrongful termination?
case_study_questions.option_a: Claim damages for breach of contract
case_study_questions.option_d: No remedy as contract is void
case_study_questions.explanation: The RP can seek remedies for wrongful termination that violates moratorium. This may include damages for breach of contract or seeking specific performance if the contract is essential for the corporate debtor's revival.
